sources.entry: Measuring an engineering organization - Will Larson

summary.title: Measuring an engineering organization
summary.one_liner: Learn to choose engineering metrics by purpose and audience (planning, operations, optimization, and inspiration, plus stakeholder asks from the CEO, finance and peer teams) rather than adopting one universal metric set.
keywords: what metrics to report to ceo
takeaways: Measure first for yourself across four buckets: planning, operations, optimization, and inspiring/aspiring.
Stakeholder requests (CEO/board, finance, strategic and tactical peer teams) usually map to a few categories and can often reuse your own metrics.
Start with quick, easy measurements and iterate; avoid trying to measure everything at once and take on one new measure at a time.
Avoid anti-patterns such as using optimization metrics to judge teams, measuring individuals, or chasing perfect data over good data.
Build confidence in data by reviewing it weekly, holding hypotheses, segmenting by region or language, and comparing objective data with team experience.
summary.summary: This unedited O'Reilly Engineering Executive's Primer chapter by Will Larson argues that engineering measurement has no single answer and must match the reason for measuring. It first lays out four internal measurement goals (plan, operate, optimize, inspire) with example metrics such as shipped projects, incident counts, API latency, and SPACE or developer surveys. It then covers stakeholder requests from the CEO and board, finance, and strategic and tactical peer organizations. The chapter closes with sequencing rules, common anti-patterns, and practices for pushing on data to get real value from it.
